subject: physics
title: Potential dividers and potentiometers
key_idea: A potential divider is two resistors in series that share a supply p.d. in proportion to their resistances. Replacing one with a thermistor or LDR makes the output depend on temperature or light. A potentiometer is a uniform wire along which the potential falls steadily, used to compare p.d.s.

blocks.text: Two resistors in series carry the same current, so the supply p.d. is shared in the ratio of their resistances. Taking the output across one of them gives a fraction of the input.

blocks.label: Potential divider
where: Vin = supply p.d. across both resistors (V)

items.text: The same current flows through both: I = Vin / (R₁ + R₂).
Vout = I R₂ = R₂ Vin / (R₁ + R₂).

diagram.alt: Change the supply p.d. and the two resistances to see the output p.d. across the second resistor.

blocks.text: Supplying a constant or variable p.d.

items: Two fixed resistors give a **constant** output p.d., smaller than the supply.
A **variable resistor** connected across the supply, with the output taken from the sliding contact, gives a p.d. that can be varied smoothly from zero to the full supply.
Connecting a load across the output lowers the output p.d., because the load is in parallel with R₂.
Vout = R₂ / (R₁ + R₂) × Vin, and V₁ / V₂ = R₁ / R₂.
The larger resistor takes the larger share of the p.d.
A load across the output reduces Vout.

sections.heading: Thermistors and LDRs in potential dividers

blocks.text: Replace one resistor with a sensor and the output p.d. now depends on temperature or light.

items.text: A rise in temperature lowers the resistance of an NTC thermistor.
A smaller share of the supply p.d. is across the thermistor.
A larger share is across the fixed resistor, so its p.d. rises.

items: The output can drive a switching circuit, for example to turn a heater off when a room is warm enough.
Swapping the positions of the sensor and the fixed resistor reverses the direction of the change.
A variable resistor in place of the fixed one sets the temperature or light level at which the circuit switches.
The p.d. across a resistor rises when its share of the total resistance rises.
A sensor's resistance falls with heat or light, so its share of the p.d. falls.

sections.heading: Potential along a wire and the potentiometer

blocks.text: A uniform wire carrying a steady current has the same resistance per unit length. The p.d. between two points on it is proportional to the distance between them.

items: A driver cell sends a steady current through a long uniform wire.
The potential falls at a constant rate along the wire, so a graph of potential against distance is a straight line.
A sliding contact therefore picks off any p.d. from zero to the p.d. across the whole wire.
This arrangement is a potentiometer, which is a potential divider with a continuously variable ratio.

blocks.text: Comparing p.d.s by a null method

items.text: Join the source to be measured, in series with a galvanometer, between one end of the wire and a sliding contact.
Slide the contact until the galvanometer reads zero. Measure the length L from the end of the wire.
Replace the source with a second one and find its balance length.
The two p.d.s are in the ratio of the balance lengths: V₁ / V₂ = L₁ / L₂.

items: At balance the galvanometer shows zero current, so the source delivers no current and there are no lost volts.
A null method compares quantities by finding a point of zero reading, which makes it very accurate. The galvanometer only needs to detect zero, not to be calibrated.
The driver cell must give a larger p.d. across the whole wire than any p.d. being compared, and the cells must face the same way.
On a uniform wire, p.d. is proportional to length.
At balance there is no current through the galvanometer, so V₁ / V₂ = L₁ / L₂.

checks.q: A 6.0 kΩ resistor and a 3.0 kΩ resistor are in series across a 12 V supply. Calculate the p.d. across the 3.0 kΩ resistor.
A thermistor is in series with a fixed resistor across a battery. Explain how the p.d. across the fixed resistor changes as the thermistor is warmed.
checks.a: Its resistance falls, so the total resistance falls and the current rises. The thermistor takes a smaller share of the supply p.d. and the fixed resistor takes a larger share, so its p.d. rises.

checks.q: A cell of e.m.f. 1.50 V balances at 62.0 cm on a potentiometer wire. A second cell balances at 41.0 cm. Calculate its e.m.f.

items: Examples must include variable resistors, thermistors and LDRs in the divider.
The use of the potentiometer as a measuring instrument is not required.

blocks.text: You must know how to investigate and design a sensor circuit.

items.text: Connect a thermistor or LDR in series with a fixed resistor across a supply, with a voltmeter across one of them.
Change the temperature (using a water bath and thermometer) or the light level, and record Vout each time.
Choose the fixed resistor so that Vout crosses the switching p.d. at the temperature or light level you want, using Vout = R₂ / (R₁ + R₂) × Vin.
